title: Reorder Balanced Bit Blocks
statement:
Call a string of 1s and 0s balanced when it has as many 1s as 0s and every prefix has at least as many 1s as 0s. Read 1 as an opening bracket and 0 as a closing one: balanced strings are exactly the well-formed bracket strings.

You get a non-empty balanced string s. In one move you pick two non-empty balanced substrings that sit right next to each other and swap them. You may make any number of moves.

Return the lexicographically largest string you can reach.

examples.why: s is "10" followed by "110100", both balanced. Swapping them puts the larger block first.
The whole string is one block "1…0" with "10101100" inside. Swapping at the top level does nothing; the gain comes from reordering the inner blocks "10", "10", "1100" into "1100", "10", "10".
There is no pair of non-empty blocks to swap.

hints: Split s into its top-level blocks: cut every time the running count of (1s − 0s) returns to 0. Swapping adjacent blocks lets you put those blocks in any order.
Each top-level block is "1" + (a balanced inside) + "0". Moves can also happen inside that inner part, independently.
Recursively make every block's inside as large as possible, then sort the top-level blocks in decreasing order and join them.

explain.intuition:
Think of s as brackets. Cutting wherever the balance returns to 0 splits it into top-level blocks, each of the form 1 X 0 with a balanced X inside. Swapping adjacent balanced pieces is like adjacent swaps in bubble sort, so the top-level blocks can end up in any order. To make the string largest, put larger blocks first: sort them in decreasing order.

A move can also act entirely inside one block's X, so first make every X as large as possible by the same rule, recursively. Sorting plain strings is safe here because no block is a proper prefix of another (a block's balance first hits 0 at its very end), so comparing two blocks decides at the first differing character.
steps: Walk s with a balance counter: +1 for 1, −1 for 0. Remember where the current block started.
Whenever the balance returns to 0, the block s[start..i] is complete. Recursively solve its inside s[start+1..i−1] and wrap the result as "1" + inner + "0".
Collect all blocks of this level, sort them in decreasing order, and join them.
The recursion bottoms out on the empty string.
pitfalls: Sorting only the top level. The second example is a single block; all of the gain is inside it.
Sorting in increasing order, or sorting individual characters. The pieces being moved are whole balanced blocks.
Cutting blocks at any place the balance is 0 inside a recursive call but passing the wrapped string (with its outer 1 and 0) down again, which recurses forever.

complexity.time: O(n²) (each level copies and sorts its substrings)
complexity.space: O(n²) worst case for the substrings

solutions.title: Search every reachable string
solutions.idea: BFS over strings: from each one, try every swap of two adjacent balanced substrings. Keep the largest string seen. Only feasible for very short inputs.

solutions.title: Split into blocks, improve each, sort descending
solutions.idea: Cut s into top-level blocks where the balance returns to 0. Recursively maximise each block's inside, then sort the blocks from largest to smallest.

followups: Return the lexicographically smallest reachable string instead. What changes?
Why is it enough to swap only adjacent top-level blocks to reach any order of them?
